claims.text: Controlled thermal annealing can nucleate nanoscale coherent precipitates in a magnetic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy.
Interfaces around nanoscale coherent precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Precipitates hinder domain-wall movement during magnetization reversal.
Stronger domain-wall pinning increases the coercive field by impeding reverse-domain nucleation or propagation.
The annealed alloy will have a higher coercive field than a matched untreated or as-quenched alloy because of pinning by newly formed precipitates.
An untreated or rapidly quenched homogeneous baseline has lower domain-wall pinning and therefore lower coercivity.
Rapid thermal annealing can alter the microstructure and anisotropy of a FeCoNi-based HEA in a way that strengthens domain-wall pinning.
The annealing treatment must avoid extensive grain growth, excessive ordering, and undesired phase transformations for the coercivity increase to hold.
Outside the suitable annealing window, the coercivity enhancement may reverse or plateau.
An inert or controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation and helps isolate coercivity changes caused by internal microstructural modification.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on precipitate size, density, distribution, alloy composition, and annealing conditions.
TEM can establish precipitate size and density, while XRD can evaluate phase purity and grain size.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase despite verified formation of the intended precipitates would falsify the proposed intervention-to-outcome relationship.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to annealing conditions without excessive grain growth or phase transformation, but the falsification rule treats observation of those off-boundary changes as falsifying the hypothesis rather than as failure to satisfy its stated conditions.
